source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.7.10 (Centering): 'Prove an analog of the Centering Lemma 2.6.8 for sub-exponential random variables X'
source_evidence.observation: The selected exercise applies to a sub-exponential random variable X and asks for the sub-exponential counterpart of the earlier centering lemma.
The required estimate is ||X - E X||_{psi_1} <= C ||X||_{psi_1}, with C written as an absolute constant by the inherited convention.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 17; printed page 30, continuing on printed page 31
source_evidence.anchor: Lemma 2.6.8 (Centering) and its proof, especially displays (2.20) and the sentence concluding the proof
source_evidence.observation: The referenced analogue states both preservation of the relevant tail class under subtraction of the mean and a norm bound; its proof uses the norm triangle inequality, a bound for the constant random variable E X, Jensen's inequality, and the p=1 moment estimate.
The exact sub-exponential norm used in the exercise is inf {t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2}; a variable satisfying any of Proposition 2.7.1(a)-(d) is called sub-exponential.

source_evidence.anchor: Proposition 2.7.1 (Sub-exponential properties), especially properties (b) and (d) and the equivalence convention in footnote 7
source_evidence.observation: Sub-exponentiality is equivalent, up to absolute changes of parameters, to linear L^p moment growth and to the one-point exponential-moment bound; in particular a sub-exponential X has finite first moment, so E X is meaningful.

source_evidence.anchor: Definition of the comparison notation a ≲ b in the proof of Lemma 2.6.8
source_evidence.observation: An 'absolute constant' is universal rather than dependent on X or its distribution: a ≲ b means a <= C b for some absolute constant C.

binders: A probability space and a real-valued random variable X on it are inherited from the chapter's probability setting. [PDF pp. 20-24; printed pp. 31-35, Proposition 2.7.1 through Exercise 2.7.10]

There is one universal absolute constant C > 0, independent of X and its law, for which the asserted centering estimate holds for every sub-exponential X. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10 displayed C; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, footnote 5]
hypotheses: X is a sub-exponential random variable, meaning that it satisfies the equivalent properties (a)-(d) of Proposition 2.7.1. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10; PDF p. 22; printed p. 33, Definition 2.7.5]

No independence, mean-zero, symmetry, or variance normalization assumption is imposed on X; centering is precisely the operation that subtracts its generally nonzero mean. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, Section 2.6.1 opening and Lemma 2.6.8]
conclusions: The centered random variable X - E X is sub-exponential. This is the class-preservation part inherited from the requested analogue of Lemma 2.6.8, and also follows from the displayed finite norm estimate because X is sub-exponential. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, 'analog of the Centering Lemma 2.6.8' and displayed estimate; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, Lemma 2.6.8]
Its exact psi-one norm obeys ||X - E X||_{psi_1} <= C ||X||_{psi_1}. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10 displayed formula]
definitions_and_conventions: The exact psi-one norm is ||Y||_{psi_1} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(|Y|/t) <= 2}. [PDF p. 22; printed p. 33, Definition 2.7.5 and display (2.21)]
E X denotes the expectation (mean) of X, and X - E X subtracts that scalar as a constant random variable. [PDF p. 17; printed pp. 30-31, Section 2.6.1 and proof of Lemma 2.6.8]
C is an unspecified positive absolute constant; no numerical or optimal value is asserted. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed estimate; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, footnote 5]
Sub-exponentiality entails the moment bound ||X||_{L^p} <= K_2 p for all p >= 1, hence integrability at p=1. [PDF pp. 20-21; printed p. 32, Proposition 2.7.1(b)]
implicit_context: The expectation and all psi-one norms are taken with respect to the same underlying probability law. [PDF pp. 20-24; printed pp. 31-35, the continuous notation in Proposition 2.7.1, Definition 2.7.5, and Exercise 2.7.10]

The exercise invokes the proof pattern of Lemma 2.6.8: triangle inequality, control of the norm of a constant by its magnitude, Jensen's inequality, and control of the first moment by the tail-class norm, now with psi-one in place of psi-two. [PDF p. 17; printed pp. 30-31, proof of Lemma 2.6.8; PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, 'analog']

details: The estimate is uniform over all sub-exponential real random variables; its absolute constant is not allowed to depend on the variable, distribution, or probability space. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed C; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, footnote 5]
The threshold in the defining exponential-moment condition is exactly 2, and the scale is inside exp(|Y|/t). [PDF p. 22; printed p. 33, display (2.21)]
Centering uses the ordinary expectation E X, not a median or any independently chosen scalar. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed X - E X]

The result does not require X itself to have zero mean; it constructs a mean-zero translate from an arbitrary sub-exponential X. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, Section 2.6.1 motivation]

The requested analogue carries the centered variable's membership in the sub-exponential class together with its quantitative norm bound. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, reference to Lemma 2.6.8 and displayed inequality; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, Lemma 2.6.8]

undebatable_constraints: The input variable X must be sub-exponential; the exercise does not claim the estimate for arbitrary integrable random variables. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10]
The centered expression is exactly X - E X. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed formula]
Both sides use the exact psi-one norm normalized by E exp(|Y|/t) <= 2. [PDF p. 22; printed p. 33, display (2.21); PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed formula]
The multiplicative factor is an absolute constant and therefore cannot depend on X. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, displayed C; PDF p. 17; printed p. 30, footnote 5]
No independence or additional distributional assumption is part of this one-variable centering result. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, complete exercise statement]

The source does not require the sharp constant or state that C = 1; it asserts only existence of an absolute-factor bound. [PDF p. 24; printed p. 35, unspecified C; PDF p. 17; printed pp. 30-31, analogous lemma's absolute-factor proof]

ambiguities.issue: Exercise 2.7.10 displays only the norm inequality while asking for an 'analog' of Lemma 2.6.8, whose wording separately says that the centered variable remains in the class.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF p. 24, printed p. 35, Exercise 2.7.10; compared with PDF p. 17, printed p. 30, Lemma 2.6.8.
ambiguities.impact: The natural source contract includes closure under centering as well as the displayed inequality. Under the finite-norm definition, closure is also a consequence of the finite displayed bound, so this does not materially create two different mathematical requirements.

ambiguities.issue: Definition 2.7.5's prose refers to the 'smallest K3 in property 3,' while the immediately following 'In other words' display (2.21) is the one-point bound corresponding structurally to Proposition 2.7.1(d), whose parameter is K4.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF p. 22, printed p. 33, Definition 2.7.5 and display (2.21), compared with Proposition 2.7.1(c)-(d) on PDF p. 20, printed p. 32.
ambiguities.impact: For this exercise the displayed definition (2.21) fixes the exact psi-one norm unambiguously; the index/prose mismatch must not be used to substitute the nonexact property-(c) parameter.

contract_plain_english: For every real-valued sub-exponential random variable X on a probability space, its expectation exists and subtracting that expectation preserves sub-exponentiality. There is a universal positive constant C, independent of X and its law, such that ||X - E X||_{psi_1} <= C ||X||_{psi_1}, where ||Y||_{psi_1} is exactly inf {t > 0 : E exp(|Y|/t) <= 2}. No independence, prior mean-zero assumption, sharp value of C, or additional distributional condition is asserted. [PDF pp. 20-24; printed pp. 31-35, Proposition 2.7.1, Definition 2.7.5/display (2.21), and Exercise 2.7.10; PDF p. 17, printed pp. 30-31, Lemma 2.6.8 and footnote 5]
